_help: Space facts (personality/knowledge.py). 'k' = lists of words that must ALL be in the question (any one list will do); 'a' = the answer.

entries.a: Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second. Precisely, two hundred and ninety nine thousand, seven hundred and ninety two.
A light year is the distance light travels in a year, about nine and a half trillion kilometres.
There are eight planets in our solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Jupiter is the biggest planet. You could fit over a thousand Earths inside it.
Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system.
Venus is the hottest planet, around four hundred and sixty degrees, thanks to its thick atmosphere. Mercury is closer to the Sun but cooler.
Uranus is the coldest planet, with temperatures dropping below minus two hundred degrees.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
Mars is called the red planet, because of the iron oxide, basically rust, on its surface.
Saturn has the famous rings, but Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have faint ones too.
Earth has one moon.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Jupiter has well over ninety known moons. The four big ones are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Saturn has well over a hundred known moons, and astronomers keep finding more. The biggest is Titan.
Ganymede, one of Jupiter's moons, is the biggest moon in the solar system. It's even bigger than Mercury.
The Moon is about three hundred and eighty four thousand kilometres from Earth.
The Sun is about a hundred and fifty million kilometres from Earth. Its light takes a little over eight minutes to reach us.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.
The Sun is an ordinary yellow dwarf star, about four and a half billion years old, holding ninety nine percent of the mass in our solar system.
The Sun is about four and a half billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.
Earth is about four and a half billion years old.
The universe is about thirteen point eight billion years old.
The Milky Way is roughly a hundred thousand light years across.
Somewhere between one hundred and four hundred billion stars, nobody can count them exactly.
The Andromeda galaxy is the nearest big galaxy, about two and a half million light years away. It's heading our way and will merge with the Milky Way in a few billion years.
Apart from the Sun, the nearest star system is Alpha Centauri, about four point three light years away. Proxima Centauri, the closest member, is a little nearer.
A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it gets too close.
A neutron star is the collapsed core of a huge star. It's only about twenty kilometres wide but heavier than our Sun. In Elite, flying through its jet cone can supercharge your next jump.
A white dwarf is the small, hot, dense core left behind by a star like our Sun when it dies. In Elite, their jet cones give a smaller supercharge than neutron stars.
A supernova is the explosion of a massive star at the end of its life. It can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Ours is the Milky Way.
A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, where new stars are often born.
A comet is a ball of ice and dust that grows a glowing tail when it gets close to a star.
An asteroid is a rocky leftover from the early solar system. Most live in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
A dwarf planet is round like a planet but hasn't cleared other objects out of its orbit. Pluto is the most famous one.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, because it hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects.
Neil Armstrong was the first person on the Moon, in July 1969, on the Apollo 11 mission. Buzz Aldrin followed him.
Yuri Gagarin of the Soviet Union was the first person in space, in April 1961.
Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union, in 1963.
Sputnik 1, launched by the Soviet Union in October 1957, was the first artificial satellite.
The International Space Station is a laboratory orbiting Earth, about four hundred kilometres up. People have lived aboard it continuously since the year 2000.
The Hubble Space Telescope has orbited Earth since 1990 and taken some of the most famous pictures of the universe.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021. It sees in infrared, so it can look through dust and back to the earliest galaxies.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object. It's now in interstellar space.
A day on Mars, called a sol, is about twenty four hours and thirty nine minutes.
A year on Mars lasts about 687 Earth days.
Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth of Earth's.
The sky is blue because air scatters blue light from the Sun more than red light.
Sunsets look red because the light has to pass through more air, which scatters the blue away and leaves the red.
Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans.
Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted, so different parts get more direct sunlight as it orbits the Sun.
Earth turns once every twenty four hours, or twenty three hours and fifty six minutes to be exact.
Earth orbits the Sun at about thirty kilometres every second.
There are twenty four hours in a day.
